title: The Process Reward Model Is Grading the Punctuation

body:
Hunter Lightman and colleagues at OpenAI opened the door with a clean comparison in 2023. On the MATH benchmark, a reward model trained on step-level human judgements beat one trained only on final-answer correctness, enough to solve 78 per cent of a representative test subset. Process supervision beat outcome supervision. By 2024 the field had scaled it: Math-Shepherd synthesised step labels from Monte Carlo rollouts to correct answers; OmegaPRM did the same with an MCTS divide-and-conquer that located the first error in a chain by binary search. The process reward model (PRM) had become the natural tool for reranking Best-of-$N$ samples, guiding beam search, and most consequentially, for supplying a dense per-step signal during RL fine-tuning. The reasoning models that arrived in late 2024 and 2025 — long chains of thought with reflection, backtracking, and the characteristic *verify-and-restart* patterns — were meant to be the showcase for this stack.

They are not. In 2026, PRMs trained on short-CoT math data fail to help, and sometimes outright hurt, when scored on reasoning-model outputs. The DeepSeek-R1 technical report is remarkably candid: in Appendix G.2 the team concluded the benefits of a PRM during their large-scale RL run were small relative to its computational cost, found model-based PRMs susceptible to reward hacking, and abandoned the approach for RL — keeping it only for test-time reranking. The EACL 2026 short paper of Dontsov et al. went further and asked *why*. They ran a sparse-autoencoder autopsy on Qwen2.5-Math-PRM and found that roughly 80 per cent of its interpretable latents fire on surface-formatting signals — whitespace, Unicode glyphs, LaTeX punctuation — rather than mathematical content.

If this is right, then the dominant verifier of mathematical reasoning in late 2026 is in substantial part grading the punctuation.

## Why this matters

PRMs sit in two places in the modern reasoning stack. At test time they rerank candidate samples or guide a beam search over partial trajectories; this is where Lightman et al. originally beat outcome supervision. At training time they supply the dense per-step reward in GRPO- or PPO-style RL updates that have largely replaced classical RLHF for reasoning tasks. The two uses have very different robustness profiles. A test-time reranker is a scalar on top of a frozen policy — a slightly biased reranker loses you a few points of pass@1 and does no further damage. A training-time dense reward lives inside the gradient; a biased reward shapes a loss landscape that drags the policy toward whatever surface pattern it rewards, and the result is Goodhart's law written across inference-time compute.

The question of whether PRMs generalise from instruct-model step distributions to reasoning-model step distributions is therefore not a benchmark detail. It is the question of whether a widely deployed verifier is driving reasoning models toward producing nice-looking text.

## The object

Fix a policy $\pi$ that produces a reasoning trajectory $\tau = (s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_T, y)$, where $s_t$ is the $t$-th step and $y$ the final answer. Let $y^\star$ be the correct answer. The *ideal* step-value function is a conditional expectation,

$$
V^\star(s_{\le t}) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi \mid s_{\le t}}\big[\,\mathbb{1}\{y = y^\star\}\,\big],
$$

the probability that the trajectory will eventually be correct given its prefix. A PRM $f_\theta(s_{\le t})$ is a learned regressor meant to approximate $V^\star$ pointwise. The three canonical training schemes differ in how they produce regression targets.

- **PRM800K / human labels.** Lightman et al. gather per-step human judgements — *correct*, *wrong*, *neutral* — on 800,000 steps. The target for $f_\theta(s_{\le t})$ is a human classification of that specific prefix.
- **Math-Shepherd / Monte Carlo labels.** From the prefix $s_{\le t}$, sample $K$ completions under a base policy; the label is the empirical fraction of completions that reach $y^\star$. This is $V^\star$'s Monte Carlo estimator at the prefix.
- **OmegaPRM / MCTS labels.** Replace $K$ independent rollouts by a search tree that reuses prefixes across evaluations, and locate the first error by binary search over the tree.

Each scheme supplies $f_\theta$ with a particular distribution of prefixes — call it $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$. $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ is defined by whoever wrote the data: PRM800K prefixes come from a GPT-4-era solution-writing style; Math-Shepherd's prefixes come from the Llama or Mistral base model whose rollouts generated the trees. Classical regression analysis says $f_\theta$ generalises to a test distribution $\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}$ only insofar as the two distributions overlap.

The reasoning-model distribution does not overlap. A long chain of thought from a reflective reasoning model has longer and more variable per-step lengths; explicit backtracking tokens and meta-comments ("wait, let me recheck"); different step boundaries, since many reasoning models do not emit numbered steps at all; and a markedly different formatting footprint — long Unicode runs, LaTeX environments, interleaved pseudo-code. Where $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}$ diverge, any feature that is cheaper to learn than mathematical content — and formatting is always cheaper — becomes the dominant explanation of the label.

## A concrete anchor

Dontsov et al. provide the sharpest piece of evidence. They evaluated seven LLMs on standard math benchmarks under PRM reranking, confirmed the systematic failure of PRMs on reasoning-model outputs, and then interpreted Qwen2.5-Math-PRM by training sparse autoencoders on its residual stream. Of the resulting interpretable latents, around 80 per cent respond to formatting signals (whitespace patterns, Unicode symbols, punctuation) rather than mathematical structure. Linear probes trained on the SAE codes separated reasoning-model vs. instruct-model outputs cleanly, confirming that the PRM has internalised a format-aware classifier that it should not need.

The mechanism is unsurprising once one looks at the training objective. A PRM minimises

$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) \;=\; \sum_{(s_{\le t},\, y_t^{\text{label}}) \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}} \ell\!\big(f_\theta(s_{\le t}),\, y_t^{\text{label}}\big),
$$

where $\ell$ is cross-entropy or an MSE on the empirical correctness rate. If $y_t^{\text{label}}$ is even weakly correlated with surface features in $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}$ — and in human-written math it is: clean, well-formatted solutions tend to be correct, because mathematically fluent people also format well — then surface features are a shortcut that pays off during training. The shortcut is a bias only when deployed on $\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}$ that has different formatting statistics. Reasoning-model outputs are exactly that: a different formatting distribution.

The intuition pump: imagine a reasoning-model trace with messy formatting but mathematically correct steps, and a short-CoT trace with pristine formatting but a subtle algebraic error. A format-biased PRM scores the first lower than the second. In Best-of-$N$ reranking it picks the wrong one. In RL training it rewards the wrong one.

The DeepSeek-R1 team seem to have hit this empirically before anyone wrote the autopsy. Their stated reasons for abandoning PRMs during large-scale RL — difficulty of defining step boundaries, difficulty of judging step correctness, and susceptibility to reward hacking — are three facets of the same surface-form confound. A verifier whose features are formatting can be exploited by a policy that produces formatting.

## Can it be fixed?

The most direct recent fix is Zhang et al.'s *Conditional Reward Modeling* (CRM) at ICLR 2026. The idea is to score each step not in isolation but conditioned on both the prefix and the trajectory's final outcome:

$$
r_t \;=\; f_\theta\!\big(s_t \,\big|\, s_{<t},\, y_{\text{final}}\big).
$$

At training time the reward model sees the final answer, so the regression target reflects the joint $(prefix, outcome)$ structure rather than just the prefix. At test time, the authors approximate the conditional expectation over possible futures. The outcome conditioning acts as a sieve on the surface-form shortcut: a nicely formatted but ultimately wrong trajectory is penalised, a messy but ultimately correct one is not. Zhang et al. report gains over existing PRMs in Best-of-$N$, beam search, and RL fine-tuning across several reasoning benchmarks.

Fanconi, Astorga, and van der Schaar take a different route. They learn a token-level dense reasoning reward via adversarial inverse reinforcement learning from expert demonstrations rather than step labels — bypassing the step-boundary annotation problem altogether and tying the reward to whatever structure the expert policy locally emits. On GSM8K with Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 backbones, the dense reward works as both a training signal and an inference-time critic, and the authors advertise it as supplying interpretable step-wise diagnostics for where logical errors occur.

Neither of these has been independently replicated at scale yet, and both inherit assumptions — CRM about the stability of the outcome label, inverse RL about the quality and representativeness of expert demonstrations — that will have their own distribution-shift stories to tell on reasoning models.

## What to do with it

The reasoning-model distribution is not what any off-the-shelf PRM was trained on. Before trusting a PRM in a reasoning RL loop, run two diagnostics the Dontsov paper makes cheap. First, a linear probe on the PRM's hidden states against a reasoning-vs-instruct binary label: if the probe reaches high accuracy, the PRM has internalised a style classifier, and the direction it reads is a confound. Second, a small SAE on the top blocks, with latents inspected on activating examples: if the top activators are formatting features, you are holding a formatting classifier that happens to correlate with correctness in training, not a verifier.

For test-time use on long reasoning traces, prefer outcome-level verifiers — ORMs, ground-truth checkers, code execution, symbolic solvers — over off-the-shelf PRMs. For training-time use, the honest default on current evidence is to supply ground-truth outcome rewards with sparse step-level shaping, or to use a conditionally trained reward (CRM-style) if density is needed. The era of dropping an off-the-shelf PRM into a reasoning RL pipeline is over.

## Limits and open questions

Several threads are unresolved. First, the surface-form confound is well-evidenced on Qwen2.5-Math-PRM but has not been audited across the full stable of 2026 PRMs; the magnitude and shape of the problem may vary with training recipe, base model, and label source. Second, CRM relies on knowing the outcome label at training time, which is routine for verified math and graded code but is not for open-ended reasoning (law, medicine, long-form science writing); the fix there is open. Third, the deeper question of whether we want a neural step-level verifier at all — DeepSeek-R1 famously dropped neural reward models for math and code in favour of rule-based verifiers, and the result that outcome-only RL can still elicit strong reasoning complicates the case for PRMs even without the surface-form confound. Fourth, the whole SAE-based diagnosis depends on the SAE itself being a faithful readout of the PRM's representations, which the recent sanity-check literature on SAEs makes conditional, not axiomatic.

The picture is less an obituary than a reset. Process supervision as a construct did real work on short-CoT math and taught the field how to think about step-level credit assignment. The thing that broke is a specific generation of PRMs trained on a specific generation of model outputs, under a specific implicit assumption of distributional overlap that reasoning models silently violated. The next generation of verifiers — conditional, demonstration-recovered, rule-grounded, or something else — will be the ones that read reasoning for what it is rather than for how it is laid out.

## Further reading

- Lightman, H., Kosaraju, V., Burda, Y., Edwards, H., Baker, B., Lee, T., Leike, J., Schulman, J., Sutskever, I., Cobbe, K. (2024). *Let's Verify Step by Step.* ICLR 2024; arXiv:2305.20050. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050>. The paper that established process supervision as the preferred signal on MATH, and released PRM800K.
- Wang, P., Li, L., Shao, Z., Xu, R., Dai, D., Li, Y., Chen, D., Wu, Y., Sui, Z. (2024). *Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations.* ACL 2024; arXiv:2312.08935. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08935>. The automated Monte-Carlo step-labelling pipeline that made large-scale PRM training feasible.
- Luo, L., Liu, Y., Liu, R., Phatale, S., Lara, H., Li, Y., Shu, L., Zhu, Y., Meng, L., Sun, J., Rastogi, A. (2024). *Improve Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models by Automated Process Supervision.* arXiv:2406.06592. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06592>. OmegaPRM, with the divide-and-conquer MCTS labelling scheme and 1.5M automatically generated step annotations.
- DeepSeek-AI (2025). *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.* arXiv:2501.12948. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>. Appendix G.2 lays out the team's reasons for abandoning PRMs and MCTS in their large-scale RL run.
- Dontsov, A., Korznikov, A., Galichin, A. V., Tutubalina, E. (2026). *Out of Distribution, Out of Luck: Process Rewards Misguide Reasoning Models.* EACL 2026 Short, pp. 421–435. <https://aclanthology.org/2026.eacl-short.31>. The 80-per-cent-of-features-are-formatting result and the SAE autopsy of Qwen2.5-Math-PRM.
- Zhang, Z., Shan, Z., Song, K., Li, Y., Ren, K. (2026). *Linking Process to Outcome: Conditional Reward Modeling for LLM Reasoning.* ICLR 2026; arXiv:2509.26578. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26578>. The CRM proposal — step rewards conditioned on prior steps and final outcome.
- Fanconi, C., Astorga, N., van der Schaar, M. (2025). *Learning Reasoning Reward Models from Expert Demonstration via Inverse Reinforcement Learning.* arXiv:2510.01857. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01857>. Token-level dense reasoning reward learned from expert demonstrations via adversarial inverse RL.
